input.contentScopeRationale: The assignment LAB-MATH-C ("Festival Team Challenge") asks the child to move between four surface forms of one idea: equal-groups word problems (items 1, 5), a missing-factor equation (items 2, 3), array structure and commutativity (items 4, 8), and interpretation/repair of multiplicative language and near facts (items 6, 7). The teacher's target is not any single fact but the underlying equal-groups structure (groups x size-of-group = total) and the ability to recognize that structure whichever way it is dressed. The smallest coherent program therefore teaches the equal-groups structure and its unknown positions, then tests independent transfer across representations, without copying the worksheet's numbers or wording. Because this child chart is empty (no prior constructs, no fact bank, no engagement events, no prior decisions), the program stays practice_only, keeps a shared teaching/baseline spine, and uses a two-route fork only to gather first engagement facts at comparable academic difficulty. Quest and Boss are deliberately excluded: there is no real evidence yet to justify a mastery gate.
input.name: Equal-groups structure of multiplication
input.statement: A multiplication situation has a number of equal groups and a size of each group; total = number of groups x size of group. The same structure can be shown as a story, an array of rows and columns, or an equation, and any one of the three quantities can be the unknown.

assumptions.claim: This child has no recorded prior performance on any multiplication construct, so every academic estimate in this plan is a prior belief from the assignment's grade level rather than from child data.
assumptions.uncertainty: The empty chart could mean a genuinely new learner or a data-transfer gap; if prior instruction exists elsewhere, the baseline may be set too low and the child may finish quickly with ceiling scores.

assumptions.claim: Grade 3 placement (age 9) makes single-digit factors within 10 x 10 the correct working range for teaching and transfer items.
assumptions.uncertainty: Grade placement does not fix actual fluency; the child may still be at repeated-addition level or may already be automatic with these facts.

assumptions.claim: The teacher's target is independent transfer of one equal-groups structure across facts, arrays, and word problems, not memorization of the eight specific worksheet answers.
assumptions.uncertainty: The worksheet is a BLANK synthetic fixture with no completed responses, so the teacher's grading emphasis is inferred from item design alone.

assumptions.claim: The most probable error patterns for this assignment profile are additive substitution for multiplicative language, treating a missing factor as a subtraction, dropping the second step in two-step equal-groups problems, and not recognizing that a rows-by-columns array yields a commutative pair.
assumptions.uncertainty: No child work exists; these are item-design-derived hypotheses, not observed misconceptions, and the first baseline node may falsify all of them.

assumptions.claim: No catalog candidate has an assignment-specific frozen academic contract or verified hash for this concept, so reuse is not eligible anywhere and every node must be revised or newly generated.
assumptions.uncertainty: Runtime registration status may change before build; if a frozen exact contract appears, a revise decision here could become a cheaper reuse.

assumptions.claim: There is no factual engagement history for this child, so neither fork route can be predicted to be more motivating and the route choice must be treated as weak evidence only.
assumptions.uncertainty: A first choice can be driven by node order, wording, or novelty; it will not distinguish a durable preference from a one-time pick.

assumptions.claim: Quest and Boss should remain locked because a mastery gate requires prior baseline evidence that does not yet exist for this child.
assumptions.uncertainty: If baseline transfer scores come back uniformly high, a quest-level transfer probe may be justified sooner than this plan assumes.

input.academicTheory: Theory: the child's performance on this assignment will be governed by whether one equal-groups schema (groups x size = total) is available and flexible, not by isolated fact recall. If the schema is only attached to the "so many groups of so many" story surface, then performance will drop specifically when (a) the unknown moves out of the product position (missing factor), (b) the structure is presented spatially as rows and columns and must be read as two equivalent equations, (c) the story language is additive or partitive rather than multiplicative, or (d) a second equal-groups step is embedded in one sentence. The program therefore teaches the schema explicitly with a shared model-building node, then measures each of those four stress points in separate baseline nodes so that a failure can be localized to a representation rather than to "multiplication" in general. A single unnamed misconception is not assumed; instead, the plan preregisters four candidate error patterns and lets the first shared node select among them. Delayed independent performance, not in-session accuracy, is the outcome of interest, and engagement facts from the fork are explicitly excluded from academic inference.

learningResponsibilities.title: Build and name the equal-groups schema
learningResponsibilities.purpose: Establish, before any transfer measurement, that the child can identify number of groups, size of group, and total in a plain situation and can say which quantity is unknown.
learningResponsibilities.academicTarget: Identify groups, group size, and total in an equal-groups situation and write the matching equation with the unknown marked.

learningResponsibilities.title: Move the unknown out of the product position
learningResponsibilities.purpose: Measure whether the schema survives when the total is known and a factor is missing, which is the assignment's items 2 and 3.
learningResponsibilities.academicTarget: Solve missing-factor problems within 10 x 10 by reasoning from the equal-groups structure rather than by guessing an operation.

learningResponsibilities.title: Read arrays as two equivalent equations
learningResponsibilities.purpose: Measure whether a spatial rows-by-columns representation is recognized as the same structure and yields a commutative equation pair and alternative factor pairs for one total.
learningResponsibilities.academicTarget: Translate an r-by-c array into both r x c and c x r, and generate more than one equal-row arrangement for a given total.

learningResponsibilities.title: Separate multiplicative language from additive and sharing language
learningResponsibilities.purpose: Measure whether story wording, including two-step equal-groups wording, is parsed structurally instead of by keyword habit.
learningResponsibilities.academicTarget: Choose or construct the equation that matches a story, rejecting additive and partitive distractors, including one embedded two-step case.

learningResponsibilities.title: Repair a wrong product using an adjacent known fact
learningResponsibilities.purpose: Measure whether the child can use structure (one more group / one less group) to check and correct a stated product, which is the assignment's item 7.
learningResponsibilities.academicTarget: Explain and apply a near-fact adjustment such as using 5 x 10 or 4 x 9 to correct a wrong value for 5 x 9.

learningResponsibilities.title: Optional low-stakes mixed consolidation
learningResponsibilities.purpose: Offer extra fresh assignment-aligned practice that carries no mastery weight and whose absence cannot block the board.
learningResponsibilities.academicTarget: Re-encounter equal-groups structure across mixed surfaces at baseline difficulty with no new content.
